'''''Persicaria decipiens''''', commonly known as '''slender knotweed''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] [[native plant|native]] to Australia and Asia.<ref name="floransw">{{NSW Flora Online|genus=Persicaria |species=decipiens|author=Wilson, K.L.|date=2014}}</ref>

''Persicaria decipiens'' is a trailing plant whose stems grow horizontally at first but become more vertical with time,<ref name=Benson2000/> reaching {{convert|30|cm|ft|0|abbr=on}} high. Its narrow elliptic to lanceolate (spear-shaped) leaves are {{convert|5|–|12|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|0.5|–|1.3|cm|in|abbr=on}} across.<ref name="floransw"/> The slender pink flower spikes appear from November to June, with a peak in February.<ref name=Benson2000/> Cylindrical in shape, they are not stiff and tend to bend over.<ref name="floransw"/> The plant tends to die back in winter and regenerate after rain.<ref name=Benson2000/>

''Persicaria decipiens'' was among the plants collected by [[Joseph Banks]] and [[Daniel Solander]] on 5 May 1770 at [[Botany Bay]] during the [[First voyage of James Cook|first voyage of Captain James Cook]].<ref name=wilson88>{{cite journal |authorlink1=Karen Louise Wilson| author=Wilson, Karen L. | journal=Telopea |title=''Polygonum'' sensu lato (Polygonaceae) in Australia | year=1988 | volume=3 |issue =2 |pages=177–82 |doi= 10.7751/telopea19884806 | bibcode=1988Telop...3..177W | url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/partpdf/281773| doi-access=free }}</ref> Prolific Scottish botanist [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] described the species as ''Polygonum decipiens'' in his 1810 work ''[[Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae et Insulae Van Diemen]]''.<ref name="Brown 1810">{{cite book | last=Brown | first=Robert | authorlink=Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773) | year = 1810 | title = Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae et Insulae Van Diemen | publisher = Richard Taylor and Company | location = London, United Kingdom |language= Latin |page=420 |url = https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/2954576}}</ref> It was given its current name by [[Karen Louise Wilson|Karen Wilson]] in 1988 as the broadly defined genus ''[[Polygonum]]'' was split into smaller genera.<ref name=wilson88/> Common names include slender knotweed, willow weed and snake root.<ref name="PROTA04">{{cite book|last=Grubben|first=G. J. H. |title=Vegetables |publisher=PROTA|date=2004|series=Plant Resources of Tropical Africa|volume=2|pages=413–14|isbn=9789057821479|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6jrlyOPfr24C&pg=PA414}}</ref>
[[File:Persicaria decipiens flowerhead7 Macquarie Marshes (16985911817).jpg|thumb|left|Flowerhead]]
''P. decipiens'' is found in water and wet soil. It is found across Africa and the Mediterranean,<ref name="PROTA04"/> through southwestern Asia, Malesia and all states of Australia, as well as Norfolk Island, New Zealand and New Caledonia.<ref name="floransw"/> It has become naturalised in Madagascar.<ref name="PROTA04"/>

Likely pollinators of its flowers are insects, including honeybees, native bees, flies, wasps and small butterflies.<ref name=Benson2000>{{cite journal|author1=Benson, Doug|author2=McDougall, Lyn|year=1999|title=Ecology of Sydney Plant Species Part 7a: Dicotyledon families Nyctaginaceae to Primulaceae|journal=Cunninghamia|volume=6|issue=2|pages=402–508 [484]|url=https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/RoyalBotanicGarden/media/RBG/Science/Cunninghamia/Volume%206%20-%201999/Volume-6(2)-1999-Cun6Ben402-509.pdf|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160313135801/https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/RoyalBotanicGarden/media/RBG/Science/Cunninghamia/Volume%206%20-%201999/Volume-6%282%29-1999-Cun6Ben402-509.pdf|archivedate=2016-03-13}}</ref>

''Persicaria decipiens'' is not cultivated but is eaten locally in times of famine in Africa.<ref name="PROTA04"/>
